episodes.text: As a small child, before being able to hold a pencil, compulsively sketched in the air with his fingers; once given a pencil, drew every day for the rest of his life -- a documented, self-directed creative habit beginning in early childhood.

After graduating architecture school in 1934, worked without pay in Lucio Costa's studio specifically to master draftsmanship under an established modernist, rather than seeking immediately paid, independent work.

Was initially excluded from Lucio Costa's high-profile Ministry of Education and Health team (which included consultant Le Corbusier) but insisted on joining; his subsequent design modifications so impressed Costa that Costa gradually ceded full project leadership to him by 1939.

Designed the Church of Sao Francisco de Assis at Pampulha using a structurally unorthodox curved-shell form that unified wall and roof, abandoning conventional pillar-beam-slab construction; the Catholic Church refused to consecrate the building for roughly 16 years because of its form and Portinari's unconventional murals, and Niemeyer did not alter the design to secure faster approval.

As the youngest member of the UN Headquarters international design board (1947-49), his own scheme 32 was initially the board's preferred design over Le Corbusier's competing scheme, even though Le Corbusier had asked him not to submit a competing design at all.

Despite his own design being the UN board's preferred scheme, yielded to sustained pressure from the more senior Le Corbusier and agreed to a merged submission combining both designs, rather than insisting the board's own preference proceed unmodified; Le Corbusier privately labeled his own sketch "beau" and Niemeyer's "mediocre" in his notebook.

His Communist Party sympathies caused U.S. visa denials that blocked a 1946 Yale teaching invitation and a 1953 Harvard Graduate School of Design deanship appointment; he did not renounce or downplay his political affiliation to secure either position.

When rationalist critic Max Bill publicly attacked his free-form curved style as merely decorative and risking "anti-social academicism," Niemeyer first denied the criticism, then produced a substantive counter-argument that Bill's framing ignored Brazil's different social and economic realities, rather than remaining silent or fully conceding the point.

In the same episode, publicly admitted he had "handled too many commissions, executing them in a hurry," leading to diluted-quality imitations of his own style, and subsequently published a manifesto ("Depoimento") deliberately simplifying his design approach -- a documented self-correction rather than defending the prior approach unchanged.

Designed and completed the entire government/civic core of Brasilia -- presidential palace, national congress, cathedral, supreme court, ministries -- within four years, working alongside his own former mentor Lucio Costa (urban plan) after being personally invited by President Kubitschek at Niemeyer's own home.

Embedded an explicit egalitarian ideology directly into Brasilia's design (government-owned apartments with no distinct "nobler" zones, ministers and laborers meant to share buildings), but in practice the city's service workers ended up housed in surrounding favelas while government employees commuted from Rio and Sao Paulo, and the car-centric layout produced empty, underused public plazas -- a documented gap between his stated design ideology and the built social outcome.

In 1945, sheltered communist militants released from Getulio Vargas's dictatorship at his own architectural office, met left-wing leader Luis Carlos Prestes through this act, and formally joined the Brazilian Communist Party the same year -- using his own professional space to materially assist people facing state repression prior to his own formal political commitment.

Sustained a decades-long, personal (not merely symbolic) friendship with Fidel Castro, who frequently visited his apartment and studio and said "Niemeyer and I are the last communists on this planet"; in 2007, at age 99-100, gave Castro a sculpture explicitly described as anti-American in content.

Served as the formal president of the Brazilian Communist Party from 1992 to 1996 (in his mid-to-late 80s), providing organizational legitimacy during the party's post-Soviet-collapse crisis -- a sustained, formal leadership commitment continuing into old age rather than a purely symbolic younger-era affiliation.

When directly confronted with the tension between his communist ideology and his career of designing palaces/cathedrals for the state and wealthy private clients, did not deny the contradiction but explicitly acknowledged it: "Architecture does not change anything. It's always on the side of the wealthy. The important thing is to believe that it can make life better."

After the 1964 military coup, his office was raided and pillaged and his clients disappeared; in 1965 he and roughly 200 University of Brasilia professors collectively resigned in protest of the government's treatment of the university, rather than continuing to work quietly within the institution.

Facing direct professional persecution (office raided, clients lost, a government minister reportedly saying "the place for a communist architect is Moscow"), left Brazil for exile in France in 1965 and rebuilt an internationally distributed architectural practice from a new Paris office over the following two decades rather than abandoning the profession or moderating his politics to return sooner.

While exiled and unable to work in Brazil, designed the headquarters of the French Communist Party in Paris, donating the design plans specifically because the PCF sought him out as an exiled, committed lifelong communist -- fusing his political identity directly into a major professional commission during his most professionally vulnerable period.

During the two-decade exile, sustained a substantial, internationally distributed client list across France, Algeria, Italy, Portugal, and Lebanon, including two U.S. commissions designed entirely by mail without ever visiting the sites, and collaborated with his own daughter Anna Maria on furniture design -- maintaining prolific creative output despite being professionally severed from his home country.

Wrote a homesick poem during his French exile expressing direct emotional longing for Brazil ("I want to watch the stars / I want to feel life / And be back in Brazil / That's where I want to live") -- first-person evidence of emotional distress during the exile period, not merely an inferred hardship.

Continued designing major international public buildings well into extreme old age -- the Serpentine Gallery Summer Pavilion in London at age 96, the Oscar Niemeyer International Cultural Centre in Spain at 103-104, and the Oscar Niemeyer Sphere in Leipzig, reportedly his final design -- rather than retiring once financially and reputationally secure.

At 91, won Britain's RIBA Royal Gold Medal but did not travel to London to accept it in person, reportedly because of a genuine fear of flying -- a specific, concrete personal limitation despite a career built substantially on remote/international commissions.

When NYT critic Nicolai Ouroussoff publicly and directly questioned whether his advanced age had degraded the quality of his late work (the Niteroi museum specifically), the criticism stood publicly contested by other named critics (e.g. Joao Masao Kamita calling it a genuine "return to form") rather than Niemeyer himself issuing any documented rebuttal -- a case of serious professional criticism of his continued output at advanced age met with public disagreement among critics, not personal defensiveness from Niemeyer.

At nearly 100 years old, described his continued daily work plainly rather than dramatizing it ("I just did my work... I tried to do the things I liked to do"), still climbing stairs each morning to a full day of work in his penthouse office with a desk full of active projects; at 101 maintained a fixed daily schedule of press meetings and continued design work rather than treating retirement as a live option.

Explicitly rejected the Bauhaus/rationalist premise that architecture's value lies purely in functionalism ("Architecture has to be pretty. It has to amaze to be a masterpiece"), maintaining a consistent, decades-long aesthetic position against the dominant rationalist critique of his own era (see also the Max Bill episode).

At 101, when directly asked whether his signature curves referenced the female body -- a claim repeated in coverage of his own furniture design and consistent with his own memoir's nature-derived curve language -- flatly denied it ("The form comes from nothing"), a documented, unresolved self-contradiction between his own earlier writing and his later interview statement.

In his own memoir's introduction, explicitly self-reported an internally acknowledged dual temperament -- one persona drawn to life's bright side, the other angered by the world's injustices -- rather than presenting a single, uncomplicated self-image.

As a lifelong atheist who reasoned explicitly from the world's injustices and a naturalistic cosmology, nonetheless designed numerous religious buildings across multiple faiths (Catholic chapels, an Orthodox church, mosques) over his career, respecting each commission's spiritual purpose despite not personally sharing the underlying belief.

Following his wife Annita's death in 2004 after 76 years of marriage, and a hip fracture from a fall, remarried in 2006 (shortly before his 99th birthday) to his longtime secretary Vera Lucia Cabreira, then 60 years old.

His daughter and former furniture-design collaborator Anna Maria died in June 2012, roughly six months before Niemeyer's own death in December 2012 at age 104 -- a documented late-life personal loss immediately preceding his own final decline.

President Dilma Rousseff hosted his funeral at the Palacio do Planalto, the presidential palace he himself designed, providing an Air Force plane to carry his body from Rio de Janeiro to Brasilia -- the highest available level of formal state honor at death, consistent with his sustained decades-long personal proximity to Brazilian political leadership since Kubitschek.
